Abstract
Based on the cross-cultural context, this paper discusses the pluralism and innovation of Sun Wukong’s image under the postmodernist interpretation. Through the analysis of the evolution and dissemination of Sun Wukong in different historical periods and cultural contexts, this paper reveals the transformation of his image from the traditional hero symbol to the complex, multi-faceted character role. In modern film and television works, network literature and animation work, Sun Wukong’s image is endowed with more personal emotion, psychological description, and modern elements, showing the characteristics of anti-heroism, hybridity, irony and parody, and cultural diversity. These characteristics not only enhance Sun Wukong's image's cultural meaning but also foster intercultural dialogue and understanding. This study illustrates the flexibility and adaptability of cultural symbols through the postmodernist interpretation of Sun Wukong’ s appearance, offering motivation for the cultural industry’ s future innovation.
Key words: Sun Wukong; Post Modernism; Cross-Cultura context; Cultural Diversity; Nti-Heroism

Chapter One Introduction
1.1 Research Background
With his distinct personality, remarkable talent, and intricate storyline, Sun Wukong, the legendary protagonist of the beloved Chinese novel Journey to the West, has become a cultural icon in China. Since the creation of Wu Chengen in the Ming Dynasty, Sun Wukong has not only been widely known in China, but also its influence transcends national borders and enjoys worldwide fame. He is smart, brave, witty and humorous, and perfectly combines the spirit of bravery, wisdom, loyalty and rebellion, adding infinite splendor to the journey, and symbolizing the national spirit of courage, wisdom and perseverance.
From traditional literature to contemporary film and television, animation, advertising, brand endorsement, and even network literature and social media, Sun Wukong’s image has long been widely used in a variety of media. Its diversified presentation not only enriches the cultural connotation, but also becomes a bridge between Chinese culture and the world culture. However, with the rise of postmodernism, Sun Wukong’s image began to experience profound changes. In this context, the portrayal of Sun Wukong shows the characteristics of authoritative resolution and parody collage. Many film and television works deconstruct the structure of the original story and the relationship between characters, integrate the personal perspective of the creator, and create the image of Sun Wukong with their own characteristics.
The contemporary interpretation of Sun Wukong's image has been greatly impacted by postmodernism, which is characterized by its artistic style of no depth, no center, no basis, self-reflection, gamification, simulation, eclecticism, and pluralism. In the cross-cultural context, Sun Wukong gradually changes from the traditional hero symbol to a complex and multi-faceted character, which is not only reflected in the external image and personality characteristics, but also goes deeper into the inner world and emotional expression. In modern film and television works, the character of Sun Wukong’s rebellion has been significantly amplified, and even has a “dark” color. For example, in A Chinese Odyssey to the West, he not only challenges the authority of heaven, but also questions his own destiny and existence significance. Such deep rebellion and self-exploration make the image of Sun Wukong more three-dimensional and real, and close to the aesthetic needs of modern audiences.
In addition, modern works give Sun Wukong more personal emotions and psychological descriptions; he is no longer a single dimension of the hero but has multiple personalities and complex emotions of the individual. This change is not only a reinterpretation of the traditional hero image but also reflects modern people’s pursuit of individuality and freedom.
1.2 The Significance and Goal of the Research
We can better understand the flexibility and malleability of cultural symbols by examining the postmodernist interpretation of Sun Wukong’s appearance. As an important symbol of traditional Chinese culture, Sun Wukong’s image has undergone constant evolution and reconstruction in different historical periods and cultural environments. The post-modern culture, with its characteristics of decentralization, diversification and fragmentation, provides new possibilities and space for the interpretation of Sun Wukong’s image. This study helps us better comprehend the complexity and diversity of cultural interactions by illuminating the ways in which cultural symbols acquire new meanings and values in various cultural contexts.
In addition, this research also has important academic value and practical significance. At the academic level, it enriches our understanding and application of postmodern cultural theories, and provides a new perspective and method for cross-cultural research. In practice, through the postmodernist interpretation of Sun Wukong’s image, we can provide beneficial inspiration and reference for the innovation and development of cultural industry. For instance, this research can give us helpful advice on how to better incorporate traditional cultural components with contemporary aesthetic principles and how to develop cultural goods that appeal to people from different cultural backgrounds when making animation, video games, and other media.
Chapter Two Theoretic Foundation
2.1 An Overview of the Theory of Postmodernism
Postmodernism theory is a complex and diversified trend of thought that originates from modernism but rebels against it. It criticizes and deconstructs the thinking modes of subjectivity, sensory richness, wholeness, centrality, and identity that emerged in the process of modernization and criticizes and deconstructs essentialism, foundationalism, and “presence metaphysics” of traditional Western philosophy.
Postmodernism theory emphasizes the rebellion and innovation of modernism. It refuses to regulate the world with unity and wholeness, opposes explaining the world with fixed logic and rules, respects differences, and advocates the coexistence of diversity. This theory advocates the elimination of depth mode towards the sense of flatness, the elimination of essence with phenomenon, the elimination of center with edge, and the elimination of reality with fiction (text). It is opposed to individualism, and pays more attention to the relationship between individuals and society, and how people should better adapt to the information and commercialization of high-tech society (Lele Qu 2024). However, postmodernism also encourages innovation because it holds that knowledge is socially constructed rather than a reaction to reality. As a result, it encourages people to fully express their creativity, challenge conventional wisdom, and look for a fresh and worthwhile perspective.
In terms of values, postmodernism shows a pluralistic form, emphasizing uncertainty, intertextuality and intersubjectivity. Rewrite these sentences, didn’t understand the means. This relativist attitude reflects the recognition of uncertainty in history and the development of things, and does not believe that there is an essential, universal, absolute truth.
In addition, the theory of postmodernism also involves the criticism of modern society. It condemns the failure of modern society to live up to its various promises and rejects such things as worldviews, wholeness, and movement and attitudes towards life as central to social development. At the same time, it gives greater importance to pre-modern phenomena such as emotion, intuition, experience, myth, and so on, rejecting the boundaries that modern society places between disciplines, between culture and life, between fiction and theory, and between imagination and reality.
2.2 Cross-Cultural Interpretation of Images
Image interpretation in a cross-cultural context is a complex and multi-dimensional process, which involves the interweaving and collision of different cultural backgrounds, values, cognitive modes, and historical experiences. In this process, images or symbols in one culture are reinterpreted and given new meanings in the context of another culture, which may even lead to misunderstandings and conflicts between cultures, but may also promote cultural exchange and integration.
Image interpretation in cross-cultural context requires a high degree of cultural sensitivity and openness (Liang Jingyu 2023:665-686). This implies that when interpreting, we should respect and recognize the distinctiveness of other cultures and refrain from imposing our own cultural viewpoints on others. To expand our own cultural perspective, we need simultaneously maintain an open mind and be prepared to accept and value new aspects and variability in other cultures.
The image interpretation in the cross-cultural context requires the use of interdisciplinary perspectives and methods. Since images often carry rich cultural connotations and symbolic meanings, it is necessary to comprehensively apply the knowledge and theories of literature, art, history, sociology, psychology and other disciplines in the interpretation. In this way, we can not only dig deeper into the cultural implication behind the image, but also more comprehensively understand the transmission and acceptance process of the image in different cultural contexts.
In addition, the image interpretation in the cross-cultural context also needs to pay attention to the differences and commonalities between cultures. Different cultures have differences in values, ways of thinking, habits of behavior, etc. These differences may lead to different interpretations of the same image. However, there are also commonalities between cultures, such as the longing for a better life and the pursuit of truth, kindness and beauty. In the process of interpretation, these commonalities should be keenly captured in order to promote mutual understanding and respect between cultures.
The process of interpreting images in a cross-cultural setting is dynamic. With the in-depth development of globalization, the communication and integration between different cultures are becoming more and more frequent, and the interpretation of images in different cultural contexts is constantly changing. As a result, in order to adjust to the evolving requirements of picture interpretation in a cross-cultural setting, we should always be aware of cultural dynamics and update our knowledge and notions.

Chapter Three The Cultural Meaning and Historical Development of Sun Wukong's Image
3.1 Origin and prototype of Sun Wukong’s image
It took a long time for Sun Wukong, a mythical character from the Chinese epic Journey to the West, to develop and become infused with many cultural components. Before Journey to the West was written, mythological characters similar to the Monkey King had been documented. In the Northern Song Dynasty, the Dunhuang murals in the Western Xia Dynasty appeared the image of a monkey following Xuanzang’s pilgrimage. In the Southern Song Dynasty (also believed to be the Yuan Dynasty), there appeared a book about Tang Monk’s Sutras. In it, there appeared a character named “Monkey Walker”. This monkey walker not only had strong magic power, but also took on the responsibility of protecting Tang Monk’s Sutras, which was considered to be one of the important sources of Sun Wukong’s image.
About the prototype of Sun Wukong, there has been a wide discussion and speculation in the academic circles and among the people. One view is that the Monkey King is based on the golden monkey from Sichuan and Yunnan provinces of China, which is famous for its golden hair, heart-shaped face and lively and cute personality, and has certain similarities with the image of Sun Wukong. Though intuitive, this assertion is not backed up by concrete data. According to another theory, the Monkey King might have been inspired by the water monster "Wu Zhiqi" of the Huai River. Wu Zhiqi is often recorded in ancient literature, and its image is “like an ape, golden eyes and snow teeth, light and swift”, which is similar to the monkey image and the fiery eyes of Sun Wukong. At the same time, Wu Zhi Qi had also stirred up trouble, obstructing the Great Yu to control the water, and then was captured and suppressed by the Great Yu, which is similar to the experience of Sun Wukong after the uproar in Heaven was suppressed by the Tathagata Buddha at the foot of the Five Elements. Mr. Lu Xun also put forward a similar view in his academic work History of Chinese Novels (Nicolle Zimmermann et al.,2024).
Furthermore, some people believe that Sun Wukong is modeled after the Indian epic Ramayana's Hanuman, the monkey deity. Hanuman went through hardships to help Rama save his wife, and Sun Wukong went through ninety-nine eighty-one difficulties to help Tang monk. At the same time, Hanuman is the Grand general of the Monkey Kingdom, and Sun Wukong is the Monkey King and the Great Sage of the Sky, both of which are similar in identity and heroic deeds. Hu Shi also put forward the view that the image of Sun Wukong comes from Hanuman in his Research on Journey to the West.
In fact, the figure of Sun Wukong probably incorporates a variety of elements and cultural backgrounds, including local Chinese myths and legends, similar characters from foreign cultures, and interpretations of folklore and artists and storytellers. These elements together constitute the cultural origin and multiple sources of the classic image of Sun Wukong.
3.2 Creating Sun Wukong's Persona in Journey to the West
Sun Wukong is a human, monkey, and divine figure in Journey to the West. He looks like a monkey, agile, lively and active, retaining much of the nature of the monkey. At the same time, he has human wisdom and emotion, can think independently, full of justice, loyal to Master Tang monk, and care for his younger brothers Zhu Bajie and Sha Seng. In addition, he also has a divine nature, with 72 kinds of changes, somersault clouds and other magical abilities, can overcome various demons and ghosts, to protect the safety of the scripture team.
In shaping the image of Sun Wukong, the author Wu Chengen skillfully uses a series of plots and details to show his character and spiritual style. Through the story of Sun Wukong, he shows his rebellious spirit of resisting authority and pursuing freedom; Through Sun Wukong’s protection of Tang Monk’s journey to the west, he shows his loyalty, bravery and heroic spirit. Through Sun Wukong’s struggle with all kinds of demons and ghosts, he shows his resourcefulness, flexibility and wisdom (Weichi Shi 2024).
The author's desire for independence, defiance of persecution, and search for the truth are also reflected in the picture of Sun Wukong. He is not bound by heaven, not limited by the teachings of Buddhism, dares to challenge authority, and pursues individuality and freedom. This spirit had a positive significance in the social background at that time, reflecting people’s dissatisfaction with the feudal autocratic rule and their desire for individual liberation.
In addition, the image of Sun Wukong also contains rich cultural connotations. He is not only an important role in ancient Chinese myths and legends, but also a symbol of wisdom and power in traditional Chinese culture. His image not only represents the ancient people’s worship of heroes and wisdom, but also reflects the ancient people’s pursuit of justice and truth.
3.3 Spread and Development of Sun Wukong's Image in Many Cultural Situations
The dissemination and evolution of the image of Sun Wukong in different cultural contexts is a complicated and interesting process, which not only reflects the changes of Chinese culture in different historical periods, but also reflects the exchange and integration of different cultures.
The character of Sun Wukong first appeared in literature and folklore in ancient China. Before Journey to the West was written, mythological characters similar to the Monkey King had been documented. With the wide spread of Journey to the West, the image of Sun Wukong has gradually penetrated into people’s hearts, and he has become a mythical hero with distinct personality and extraordinary ability. He is witty, brave, rebellious, possessed of 72 magic spells and a golden staff, all of which make Sun Wukong one of the most charming characters in traditional Chinese literature.
Into the modern era, the image of Sun Wukong began to cross the national border and go to the world. In the western perspective, the image of Sun Wukong is not unchanged, but gradually evolves with the spread and interpretation of culture. In the early English and American missionary translations, Sun Wukong was only a supporting role, but with the development of German Sinology, Sun Wukong gradually became the leading role. This change not only reflects the western understanding and construction path of Chinese culture, but also reflects the complex relationship between Eastern and Western cultures in the collision and mutual learning.
In Western culture, the image of Sun Wukong is endowed with more divine and heroic qualities. For example, the German Sinologist Willey-Hsien compiled Chinese Folk Tales with Sun Wukong as the main character, significantly elevating his status in Western culture (Bizhanhe,2023). At the same time, the depiction of Sun Wukong by western artists is also different, some highlight his animal nature, and some give hero characteristics, which further enriches the image of Sun Wukong in Western culture.
With the in-depth development of globalization, Sun Wukong’s image has further crossed the dimensional wall and is active in emerging cultural fields such as animation and games. In these fields, the image of Sun Wukong has been given more modern 0
and innovative elements, and has become a more diversified and three-dimensional cultural symbol. For example, in the "Dragon Ball" series, Monkey King is set as a super soldier with Saiyan blood, and his passionate battle scenes and warm and moving friendship stories have sparked a global craze.
The way that Sun Wukong's image spreads and changes across cultural contexts is a dynamic process. It not only reflects the changes and development of Chinese culture in different historical periods but also reflects the exchange and integration of different cultures. In this process, the image of Sun Wukong has been continuously endowed with new connotations and meanings, and has become a cultural symbol that crosses national boundaries and times.
3.4 Sun Wukong's Image's Cultural Significance and Worth
Sun Wukong is a symbol of humanity's unwavering quest for knowledge and independence. Since he was born, he has been unwilling to be bound by any constraints, boldly breaking into the dragon Palace and making trouble in the underworld, showing his resistance to established rules and his insistence on free will. This desire for freedom reflects the deep human instinct for freedom and self-actualization. At the same time, he is clever, witty, with wisdom and courage to overcome one difficulty after another, become the embodiment of wisdom and power.
The growth course of Sun Wukong also contains profound cultural connotation of self-transcendence and practice. From the initial ignorance and willfulness, to the later suffering on the way to the sutras, he gradually became mature, stable and responsible, and completed the transformation from “demon” to “Buddha”. This process symbolizes the process of constantly overcoming one’s own shortcomings and improving oneself on the road of life. It teaches us to have the courage to face their own shortcomings, through continuous learning and sharpening, to achieve spiritual sublimation and personality improvement (Chenhoujun 2023).
Furthermore, Sun Wukong is a symbol of courage and righteousness. On the way, he brought down demons, and protected the four Tang monks, masters and apprentices to overcome numerous obstacles. In the face of powerful monsters, he never flinches, always stands up, and conquers evil with fearless courage and superb skill. This quality of justice and courage has become the spiritual force that inspires people to stick to the right path and go forward in the face of difficulties and injustice.
From the perspective of cultural value, the image of Sun Wukong has been deeply integrated into the cultural gene of the Chinese nation. He became a symbol of courage, wisdom, justice and freedom, influencing generations of Chinese people. His story is not only widely circulated in China, but also attracted attention around the world, playing an important role in spreading Chinese culture (Fengjing 2024).
In the contemporary society, the cultural connotation and value of Sun Wukong still have important enlightenment significance. His quest for freedom reminds us to value our freedoms and defend our rights; His spirit of self-transcendence inspires us to continue to forge ahead and surpass ourselves; His righteous and courageous qualities inspire us to stand up and stick to the moral bottom line in the face of evil and difficulties.

4.1 Sun Wukong's Image Deconstruction From a Postmodernist Standpoint
Postmodernist works often subvert and reshape the image of classic literature by dispelling authority, reconstructing stories, and emphasizing individual feelings. In the image of Sun Wukong, this deconstruction is particularly obvious.
In “A Chinese Odyssey to the West”, the deity of Sun Wukong (the Supreme treasure) is greatly dissolved, replaced by a more distinct human nature and demon. For example, the Supreme Treasure shows strong personal feelings and desires when faced with the choice between love and learning mission. He said: “Once a true love was placed in front of me, I did not cherish it, and when I lost it, I regretted it too much. The most painful thing in the world is this” (Fanrong 2024). This passage deeply reveals the emotional struggle and desire for love in the heart of the Supreme Treasure, in sharp contrast to the divine image of Sun Wukong in the original book.
Postmodernist works also deconstruct the image of Sun Wukong by subverting the traditional mentoring relationship. In A Chinese Journey to the West, the relationship between Tang Monk and Sun Wukong is no longer the traditional mentoring relationship but becomes more complex and diversified. For example, in order to save Bai Jingjing, the Supreme Treasure repeatedly used the Moon Treasure Box to travel through time and space and even clashed with the Tang monk. During one confrontation, the Supreme Treasure said to the Tang monk, “What’s the fuss! Do you realize that you have committed a terrible crime, do you realize how many innocent people you have killed?” (Kongdegang 2023) This passage not only reflects Zhunbao’s boredom and dissatisfaction with Tang Monk, but also implies the subversion and reconstruction of the mentoring relationship.
The image of Sun Wukong is also deconstructed in postmodernist works through collage and the displacement of time and space. In “A Chinese Odyssey to the West”, the confusion and collage of time and space make Sun Wukong’s story more complex and diversified. For example, in the process of traveling through time and space, the Supreme Treasure encounters himself and other characters at different points in time, and the dialogue and interaction between these characters constitute the unique narrative structure of the film. Among them, the Supreme Treasure’s affectionate confession in the face of Zixia Fairy: “Once there was a sincere love in front of me, I did not cherish...” (Liuliang 2024) This passage not only reflects the Supreme Treasure’s persistence and pursuit of love, but also makes the image of Sun Wukong more three-dimensional and diversified through the confusion and collage of time and space.
The post-modernist interpretation of Sun Wukong's image in a cross-cultural setting highlights his humanity and demon while dispelling his divinity. The mentoring relationship is subverted and reconstructed; Time and space confusion and collage make Sun Wukong’s story more complex and diversified. These deconstruction techniques not only enrich the image connotation of Sun Wukong, but also provide the audience with more diversified interpretation and imagination space.

4.3 An Analysis of Sun Wukong's Image's Postmodernist Aspects
4.3.1 Anti-heroism
One of Sun Wukong's postmodernist characteristics in the cross-cultural setting is his propensity for anti-heroism. This trait has been extensively mirrored and expanded upon in contemporary cultural works, particularly in animation, television, and film.
An iconic figure from Journey to the West, Sun Wukong was once a courageous, clever, and devoted hero with a strong spirit of revolt, which was primarily manifested in the uprising against injustice. Modern paintings, on the other hand, portray an anti-heroic quality by amplifying and even adding extra "dark" colors to this rebellious attitude.
Take the movie “A Chinese Odyssey to the West” as an example, the image of Sun Wukong has been completely interpreted. In this film, Sun Wukong not only fights against the authority of heaven, but also questions his own destiny and the meaning of his existence. He is no longer the single, perfect hero, but an individual with multiple personalities and complex emotions. He faced his own weaknesses and mistakes, and his heart was full of contradictions and struggles. This deep rebellion and self-exploration make the image of Sun Wukong more three-dimensional and real, but also more in line with the aesthetic needs of modern audiences.
In the film, Sun Wukong’s classic lines: “Once there was a sincere love in front of me, I did not cherish it, until the time of loss was too late to regret, the most painful thing in the world is this. If God can give me a chance to do it again, I will say three words to that girl: ’I love you’. If I have to put a time limit on this love, I hope it is - ten thousand years!” (Maojie 2023) It reflects his inner tenderness and contradiction. This line not only shows Sun Wukong’s desire and regret for love, but also reflects his helplessness and struggle against his own fate.
In addition, in Monkey King: Monkey King Is Back, Sun Wukong is portrayed as a hero who has experienced a long period of loneliness and pain. He must not only fight in the face of external enemies, but also overcome inner fear and despair. This display of the inner world also makes the image of Sun Wukong more rich and moving, but also allows the audience to better understand and resonate.
4.3.2 Promiscuity
The image of Sun Wukong in modern culture presents a remarkable mix. This hybridity is not only reflected in the multifaceted nature of his character but also in the multiple interpretations and reconstructions of his image. In the original story of Journey to the West, Sun Wukong is a brave, witty, loyal, and rebellious mythological figure. However, in modern postmodernist works, Sun Wukong’s image has been given more complexity and multifacetedness.
For example, in the movie A Chinese Odyssey to the West, the image of Sun Wukong is completely subverted. He is no longer the all-powerful, honest and brave “Monkey King”, but is portrayed as a selfish, cowardly and unscrupulous low-level person. This subversive way of shaping breaks the traditional “divine” image of Monkey King, and makes the image of Sun Wukong present a kind of hybrid. He must not only fight in the face of external enemies, but also overcome inner fear and despair. This display of the inner world makes the image of Sun Wukong richer and moving. His image is no longer simple, but contains a variety of emotional elements such as bravery, tenacity, loneliness and pain.
4.3.3 Irony and parody
Sun Wukong is a well-known figure from Journey to the West, and postmodernist works frequently employ his image for satire and parody. This method exposes a number of inconsistencies and issues in contemporary society in addition to shattering the conventional hero image.
For example, in the movie “A Chinese Odyssey to the West”, the image of Sun Wukong is given the color of irony. He was originally a powerful, all-powerful hero, but in the film, he is portrayed as a poor man, powerless to change his fate. This kind of ironic shaping not only allows the audience to see another side of Sun Wukong, but also causes the audience to think about the real society. In the film, Sun Wukong no longer fights bravely against the authority of heaven, but chooses to escape and compromise. This parody of the hero image not only subverts the traditional heroic narrative, but also reveals the helplessness and powerlessness of modern people in the face of authority.
In addition, in the Biography of Wukong, another postmodernist work, Sun Wukong’s image is also used as a parody. In the film, he is no longer the brave and fearless hero who pursues freedom, but a tragic figure who is bound by heaven and cannot escape his fate. His confrontation with heaven is no longer a simple contest between justice and evil, but a profound reflection on fate and freedom. In terms of dialogue, Sun Wukong’s lines are also full of elements of irony and parody. The irony and parody features of Sun Wukong’s image in the post-modernism works are embodied in the subversion of the hero image, the revelation of the real society and the profound thinking of fate and freedom. This feature not only allows the audience to see another side of Sun Wukong, but also causes the audience to reflect deeply on modern society.

As a classic cultural symbol, Sun Wukong’s image not only occupies an important position in Chinese culture, but also has a wide influence on the world. In the Chinese cartoon Monkey King: Monkey King is Back, Monkey King says to Jiang Liuer: "If you have any difficulties in the future, call Monkey King, and I will appear." This sentence not only reflects the heroic plot of Sun Wukong to save the beauty, but also shows his modern image as a guardian, which is a re-shaping of the traditional image of Sun Wukong.
In the online novel "Fighting God of War", Sun Wukong faces the enemy and says: "I am the King of Heaven, you these small characters, also dare to be bold in front of me?" This confidence and arrogance, although retaining the character characteristics of the original, but in the environment of online literature, more emphasis on personality and heroism.
In the cartoon “Monkey King: Monkey King is Back”, Sun Wukong said to the goblins: “You demons and ghosts, all listen to me, this world is not a place where you can do wrong!” This sentence embodies Sun Wukong’s sense of justice and determination to protect the weak, as well as a modern interpretation of the traditional hero image (Yuanxue 2024).
These dialogue examples in network literature and animation show the richness and innovation of Sun Wukong’s image under the post-modernist interpretation. Through the deconstruction and recombination of traditional images, Sun Wukong’s images become more diversified and in line with modern aesthetics, reflecting the post-modernism’s re-creation of classical cultural elements and cross-cultural dialogue.
5.3 Sun Wukong's Image Transmission in Cross-Cultural Communication
The spread of Sun Wukong's image in cross-cultural communication exemplifies postmodernism, particularly the conversation instances in films and television shows with many cultural origins, which demonstrate the image's globalization and diversity.
In the Disney animated film Mulan, although it is not directly about the Monkey King’s work, there is a line in the film: "Flexible as a monkey", the metaphor here is clearly influenced by the image of Sun Wukong, showing his influence in Western culture.
In the movie Kung Fu Panda, the protagonist panda Po says, "I am a monkey. Monkeys are the most flexible!" The monkey image here is obviously a tribute to Sun Wukong, integrating the characteristics of Sun Wukong into a completely different cultural background, reflecting the image transmission in cross-cultural communication (Yuanxue 2024).
In the Netflix animated series Stranger Things, the character Dustin says, "I need courage like Son Goku," when facing danger. This statement shows that Sun Wukong’s image has been deeply rooted in people’s hearts and even had an impact in American pop culture.
In the Japanese anime Seven Dragon Ball, Sun Goku (Sun Goku is called “Sun Goku” in Japanese) often says, “I am Saiya, I will not lose to anyone!” This indomitable spirit echoes the image of Sun Wukong in Journey to the West, but finds a new interpretation in Japanese culture (Yancanwei et al.,2022).
In the international version of the film Journey to the West, Sun Wukong’s line is translated as: “I am the great Monkey King, and I will not bow down to any demon!” This way of translation and communication makes the image of Sun Wukong more international, while retaining the original cultural characteristics.
The dissemination of Sun Wukong’s image in cross-cultural communication is not only a direct translation or copy of the original work, but also a cultural re-creation and integration. Through the dialogue examples in different film and television works, the image of Sun Wukong has crossed the cultural boundary and become a global cultural symbol, which reflects the characteristics of postmodernism’s resolution of tradition and boundary.
Conclusion
The postmodernist interpretation of Sun Wukong’s image in the cross-cultural context demonstrates cultural plurality, confusion, irony, and parody. These characteristics make the image of Sun Wukong more three-dimensional and richer in the context of post-modernism. In his post-modernism works, Sun Wukong presents the characteristics of anti-heroism, subverts the traditional hero image, shows multiple personalities and complex emotions, and satisfies the aesthetic needs of modern audiences. The hybridity of Sun Wukong is reflected in the multifaceted nature of his character and the multiple interpretations of his images. Sun Wukong, for instance, is subversively shown in A Chinese Odyssey to the West as a self-centered, avaricious, and simple-minded low-level figure, breaking the conventional picture of a “divine” Monkey King. Sun Wukong’s post-modernism works also have the features of irony and parody. Through the parody of Sun Wukong, the work reveals the contradictions and problems of modern society, such as helplessness and powerlessness in the face of authority. The postmodern interpretation of Sun Wukong’s image shows the cultural diversity. In the context of globalization, Sun Wukong is no longer a single, fixed cultural symbol, but a multiple image that integrates different cultural elements. This cross-cultural integration makes the image of Sun Wukong more three-dimensional and diversified.
